newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION - Inside Canberra - Wik worries.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION - Inside Canberra - Wik worries.

text.p: Prime Minister John Howard last week declared he hoped to be able to announce by Easter the way in which the government would handle the High Court's Wik judgement.
Having attended the special meeting of the federal council of the National Party in Sydney, "Inside Canberra" believes Howard hasn't much leeway.
The mood of the federal council was a mixture of deep anger and sharp anxiety about Wik and the future of its constituents on pastoral leases throughout Australia.
Government by press release will not suffice.
Howard will need to follow up his announcement of what he intends to do with some form of positive action.
The problem is that no clear answer has yet emerged.

It should be emphasised the problem is certainly not of Howard's making and the former Keating government grievously hurt Australia by falsely claiming, even in the preamble of the Native Title Act 1993, that pastoral leases extinguish native title.
The Wik judgement says this is not so.
The National Party unanimously passed a resolution which sought for pastoral lease owners the right to convert the tenure to freehold, thus extinguishing native title, without additional cost.
Where native title existed an easement would be granted to allow native title holders to continue to exercise such rights of access they exercised up to the time of the conversion to freehold.
Legal advice given to Aboriginal groups is that pastoralists can continue to manage pastoral leases as they like without any inhibitions from native title.
Therefore, this advice says, it is not necessary to remove native title.
But a majority of senior legal opinion is that the Wik judgement did raise very serious issues about land management.

For example, if native title allowed fishing rights on a certain pastoral lease, would the lease holder be able to say to the native title holders it is not convenient for the fishing rights to be exercised at this time -- go away and come back in a week?
The problem with the National Party resolution is that it won't work.
Top legal opinion is that legislation which proposed to put into effect the National Party answer would be defeated in the High Court.
In short, the legislative approach of extinguishing native title will not work (even if it passed the Senate), because the High Court would not have a bar of it.
And in any case the agonies of trying to legislate away native title would not be worth it and would not be of lasting validity.
Some future government could legislate native title back into existence.
A referendum would also be terribly divisive and again, legislation for a referendum would be subject to the fiat of the Senate.
The legal view now gaining considerable support is that the issue has to be handled by negotiation between the parties.

But holders of this view readily admit the huge difficulty is how to clinch a deal with the appropriate Aboriginal groups which will stick long term and not be turned over by some rival Aboriginal group.
And of course the negotiation process will take a lot of time -- which is something the National Party says it is not prepared to allow.
(From the "Inside Canberra" newsletter)
-- Inside Canberra 61-6 273 1600
